intro.headline: India in 1920
intro.summary: Highlights of this year's checked items: Non-co-operation is launched; Government of India Act 1919; Srinivasa Ramanujan; Dinkarrao Shinde, fourth; The Saha ionisation equation; Nala Damayanti.

technology-science.title: Technology & science
technology-science.standfirst: In this section: The Saha ionisation equation; Tata hydroelectric power; Steel at Jamshedpur; Raman and the Calcutta laboratories.

items.title: The Saha ionisation equation
items.summary: Meghnad Saha's work on the thermal ionisation of elements produced the equation, dated about 1920, that lets astronomers relate a star's spectrum to its temperature.

items.title: Tata hydroelectric power
items.summary: The Tata hydroelectric company commissioned its Khopoli plant in 1915 and a second at Bhivpuri in 1919, bringing hydro power from the Western Ghats to Bombay.

items.title: Steel at Jamshedpur
items.summary: The Tata Iron and Steel Company began producing pig iron in 1911 and steel in 1912 at Jamshedpur, and kept working through the First World War.

items.title: Raman and the Calcutta laboratories
items.summary: C. V. Raman became the first Palit Professor of Physics at the University of Calcutta in 1917, and research scholars from several universities worked under him at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science.

government-politics.title: Government & politics
government-politics.standfirst: In this section: Viceroy: Lord Chelmsford; Government of India Act 1919; Dyarchy in the provinces; The first elections under the Act.

items.title: Viceroy: Lord Chelmsford
items.summary: Frederic Thesiger, Viscount Chelmsford, took office as Viceroy and Governor-General on 4 April 1916 and was Viceroy throughout 1920.

items.title: Government of India Act 1919
items.summary: The Act turned the Imperial Legislative Council into a two-chamber legislature: a Legislative Assembly of 145 members (104 elected) and a Council of State of 60 (34 elected).

items.title: Dyarchy in the provinces
items.summary: In the provinces some subjects, such as education, health and agriculture, were 'transferred' to Indian ministers; law and order, finance and land revenue stayed 'reserved' to the Governor.

items.title: The first elections under the Act
items.summary: 104 seats were contested for the new Legislative Assembly. Congress, which had adopted non-co-operation, did not field candidates.

children.label: Viceroy and Governor-General
children.role: Head of the Government of India

children.label: Provincial governments
children.role: Dyarchy: reserved subjects under the Governor, transferred subjects under Indian ministers

steps.label: Report
steps.detail: The Montagu–Chelmsford report, by the Secretary of State and the Viceroy, recommended wider Indian participation in government.

steps.label: Act
steps.detail: The Act received royal assent on 23 December 1919.

steps.label: Elections
steps.detail: A bicameral central legislature was elected; Congress, following Gandhi, did not field candidates.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Secretary of State for India

freedom-history.title: Independence & history
freedom-history.standfirst: In this section: Non-co-operation is launched; The All India Trade Union Congress; National institutions of education; Death of Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

items.title: Non-co-operation is launched
items.summary: The Non-cooperation movement was launched by Gandhi on 1 September 1920. A Congress session in September endorsed his proposal of swaraj through non-co-operation with British rule.

items.title: The All India Trade Union Congress
items.summary: The All India Trade Union Congress was founded in Bombay in October 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president.

sources.label: Wikipedia: All India Trade Union Congress

items.title: National institutions of education
items.summary: Within weeks of one another: the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College became Aligarh Muslim University (14 September), Gujarat Vidyapith opened at Ahmedabad (18 October) and Jamia Millia Islamia was established at Aligarh (29 October).

items.title: Death of Bal Gangadhar Tilak
items.summary: Tilak, called Lokmanya by his followers, one of the 'Lal Bal Pal' triumvirate of nationalists, died on 1 August 1920.

personalities.title: Famous personalities
personalities.standfirst: In this section: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi; Bal Gangadhar Tilak; Srinivasa Ramanujan; Meghnad Saha; C. V. Raman.

items.title: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
items.summary: Leader of the Congress's new mass movement, born in Porbandar in 1869.
items.whyThisYear: He launched the non-co-operation movement on 1 September 1920.

items.title: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
items.summary: Nationalist and journalist from Ratnagiri, born in 1856.

items.title: Srinivasa Ramanujan
items.summary: Mathematician from Erode, born in 1887, Fellow of the Royal Society since 1918.
items.whyThisYear: He died on 26 April 1920 aged 32; his last letters to G. H. Hardy, written in January 1920, still held new ideas.

items.title: Meghnad Saha
items.summary: Astrophysicist, born in 1893.
items.whyThisYear: His thermal-ionisation equation is dated to about 1920.

items.title: C. V. Raman
items.summary: Physicist, born in Tamil Nadu in 1888.
items.whyThisYear: He held the Palit Chair of Physics at Calcutta and supervised research scholars from several universities.

items.title: Lala Lajpat Rai
items.summary: Punjab leader, born in 1865.
items.whyThisYear: He returned from the United States, was elected president of the Calcutta special session of Congress and became first president of the AITUC.

sources.label: Wikipedia: All India Trade Union Congress

items.title: Premchand
items.summary: Hindi and Urdu novelist, born in 1880.
items.whyThisYear: His first major novel, Seva Sadan, had appeared in Hindi in 1919; Gandhi's call to resign government posts reached him in February 1921.

items.title: Purma Bannerjee
items.summary: Sprinter who carried the flag for India at the Antwerp Olympics.
items.whyThisYear: He ran the 100 m and 400 m at the 1920 Olympics.

items.title: A tool for reading starlight
items.summary: Saha's ionisation equation, from about 1920, remains a basic tool for interpreting the spectra of stars.

items.title: An Indian team at Antwerp
items.summary: Five Indian athletes in two sports went to the 1920 Olympics. The freestyle wrestler Dinkarrao Shinde finished fourth.

items.title: Ramanujan's lost notebook
items.summary: In his last months Ramanujan wrote down discoveries that became known as his 'lost notebook'; in his lifetime he compiled nearly 3,900 results.

items.title: A national labour federation
items.summary: The AITUC became the first federation of trade unions across India.

items.summary: In India's debut in Olympic wrestling, Dinkarrao Shinde won his quarterfinal, lost the semifinal and the bronze-medal match, and finished fourth in the freestyle featherweight class.

items.summary: Phadeppa Chaugule finished 19th in the Olympic marathon; his team-mate Sadashiv Datar did not finish.

books-reading.title: Books & reading
books-reading.standfirst: In this section: Young India; Navajivan; Saraswati; Seva Sadan.

items.title: Young India
items.summary: Gandhi's English-language periodical, published from 1919 to 1931.
items.creator: Mohandas Gandhi

items.title: Navajivan
items.summary: Gandhi's Gujarati periodical Navajivan was published from Ahmedabad from 1919; one account says it began as a monthly and became a weekly on 7 September 1919.
items.creator: Mohandas Gandhi

sources.label: Mahatma Gandhi Foundation (mkgandhi.org): Journals by Mahatma Gandhi

items.title: Saraswati
items.summary: The Hindi monthly Saraswati: Mahavir Prasad Dwivedi edited it from 1903 to 1920 and gave a platform to writers such as Premchand.
items.creator: Mahavir Prasad Dwivedi (editor)

items.title: Seva Sadan
items.summary: Premchand's first major novel was written in Urdu as Bazaar-e-Husn but first published in Hindi, in 1919, by a Calcutta publisher who offered him Rs 450.
items.creator: Premchand
